Partnering with local utilities at home and abroad could help clarify these entities’ challenges and improve cybersecurity. Electrification further blurs the traditional divide between installation energy and operational energy. Maintaining strict separation between the two can create artificial silos that hinder integrated energy strategies. For instance, a microgrid on a military base could potentially serve 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. both installation and operational energy demands, including flight lines, battery-powered unmanned aerial vehicles, and forward-operating systems. Coordinating with local grid operators, maintaining installation microgrids, and using point-of- need generation technologies could mitigate this risk. 2.2 Control System Communication Requirements Advanced energy systems depend on reliable and regular communications between digital control systems and distributed energy assets to balance load, maintain voltage, and manage peak load. These digital systems and communications from a rapidly increasing number of distributed energy generation assets expose energy systems to new cyber threats, which could shut down power provision or create uneven power supply to DOW installations. This type of vulnerability allows adversaries to target energy infrastructure remotely, complicating attribution and lowering the threshold for disruptive action. In addition, asset owners and operators (e.g., utilities, individual “prosumers,” and private energy generation companies) vary in their cybersecurity maturity, and nonuniform cybersecurity by these stakeholders could allow cyberattacks to disrupt grid reliability. Effective cybersecurity measures can be cost-prohibitive for some installations, and there are few established standards or incentives for stakeholders to prioritize cybersecurity over other investments, such as reliability or performance. Insufficient information sharing on cyber threats, vulnerabilities, and mitigation strategies remains a challenge (DOE EERE 2020). Certain adversaries and state-sponsored groups exhibit patterns of cyber-targeting critical advanced energy supply chains and infrastructure, and cyber incidents targeting digital components and communications of all energy systems are expected to increase in both sophistication and frequency (DOJ 2024; DOE EERE 2020). These risks could be intensified by reliance on products from companies headquartered in adversarial countries and further amplified by the involvement of multiple parties from construction to decommissioning, complicating efforts to maintain effective cybersecurity practices throughout the supply chain and system life cycle (DOE EERE 2020). Moreover, the management systems used to maximize the benefits of advanced energy technologies require advanced monitoring and control. For example, management systems for offshore wind plants rely on satellite communications for remote monitoring and control, creating vulnerabilities to cyberattacks. The U.S. government assessed that Russia launched cyberattacks on commercial satellite communication networks as part of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022 (Blinken 2022). This attack disrupted a major German energy company’s access to more than 5,800 wind turbines (CyberPeace Institute 2022). The integration of distributed energy resources (DERs) also involves the collection and transmission of data related to energy usage and generation, creating potential privacy concerns for DOW. Adversaries could exploit these data to assess vulnerabilities or predict energy consumption patterns of defense-critical infrastructure.
